The Đông Sơn people were skilled bronze casters, as the drums found widely through northern Vietnam and in Yunnan and Guangxi show. Bronze drums were made in large numbers in northern Vietnam, Laos and parts of Yunnan. The founders used lost-wax casting, a technique based on Chinese practice, but the scenes on the drums are local: drummers and other musicians, warriors, rice processing, birds, deer, war vessels and geometric designs.

Heger I drums carry detailed decoration around a central sun, with model frogs on the drumhead. Heger II drums, also called Li Lao drums, share the frogs and radiating sun but are much larger and decorated more plainly. According to the Lịch Sử Cổ Đại Việt Nam, the high lead content of Đông Sơn bronzes is what sets them apart from Chinese bronzes, and drums from Guangxi and Yunnan contain less lead than those of the Red River Plain.

Other bronzes show wider links: some Đông Sơn bronze daggers closely resemble Scytho-Siberian styles.

The Igbo-Ukwu culture is known from three sites in a town of south-eastern Nigeria: a shrine, a burial chamber and a cache, first dated to the 9th century CE and possibly used for several centuries. Its smiths cast finely detailed lost-wax bronzes from nearby ores, and its people traded for beads that came from as far as Egypt, Mesopotamia and Iran. The finds overturned colonial assumptions about early African art.

Kerma stood between Egypt and the African interior and passed luxury goods from Central Africa to Egypt. Egypt coveted its gold, cattle, milk products, ebony, incense and ivory. The Gash Group of eastern Sudan and Eritrea was in contact with Kerma throughout its history, and its main site, Mahal Teglinos, became an important trading partner. By 2300 BCE the C-Group culture appeared in Lower Nubia, probably from the Dongola Reach near Kerma. As Egypt’s Old Kingdom collapsed, Kerma expanded north to Aswan.

Under the Middle Kingdom, Egypt campaigned in Lower Nubia, possibly to check Kerma, and Senusret I built forts at Ikkur, Quban, Aniba, Buhen and Kor to guard the border and the gold mines of Wadi Allaqi. Kerma strongly fortified Sai, its border with Lower Nubia. When Egyptian power weakened in the Second Intermediate Period, Kerma reached its height, absorbed the kingdom of Sai and allied with the Hyksos. An inscription in the tomb of Sobeknakht II at Nekheb records that Kerma invaded deep into Egypt between about 1575 and 1550 BCE.

The New Kingdom struck back. Thutmose I led several campaigns south that destroyed Kerma and ended in Egypt’s annexation of Nubia around 1504 BCE, with a frontier at Kanisah Kurgus beyond the Fourth Cataract. Rebellions continued for about 220 years, until around 1300 BCE.

Religion appears to have been of considerable importance. At Yaoshan in Zhejiang archaeologists excavated an elaborate altar built of carefully positioned piles of stones and rock walls. It has three levels, the highest a platform of rammed earth, with three further platforms paved with cobblestones and the remains of a stone wall. On the altar lie twelve graves in two rows.

The finest pieces are large ritual jades: cong, the tube-shaped cylinders, the largest weighing 3.5 kg; bi discs; and yue ceremonial axes. They were often incised with the motif known as the taotie and were placed in elite graves, and utensils for ritual purposes have been found both inside and outside the city.

Some scholars claim that the ritual sacrifice of slaves was part of Liangzhu tradition. The influence of Liangzhu ritual objects lasted well beyond the culture itself: its jade work is said to have influenced ritual objects in later periods of Chinese culture.

At the centre of Mapuche cosmology is the creator Ngenechen, who is embodied in four parts: an old man, an old woman, a young man and a young woman. The Mapuche speak of worlds known as the Wenu Mapu and the Minche Mapu, and of spirits who live alongside people and animals in the natural world: the Pillan and Wangulen, ancestral spirits; the Ngen, spirits of nature; and the wekufe, evil spirits. Prayer and animal sacrifice have been part of ritual to keep the balance of the cosmos. Like many peoples they tell of a great flood, in which Kai Kai, the waters, fought Tren Tren, the dry earth, until order was restored.

The best-known ceremony is the Ngillatun, “general prayer”, a communal event of great spiritual and social importance; others are kept within the family. We Tripantu is the Mapuche New Year. Central to belief is the machi, a healer and spiritual specialist, usually a woman who has served an apprenticeship with an older machi. The machi performs ceremonies to cure illness, ward off evil and influence the weather and harvests, works with dreams, and knows medicinal herbs, sacred stones and sacred animals; the main healing ceremony is the machitun. A chronicle of 1673 also describes male machi weye, who wore women’s clothing.

Archaeology adds glimpses of older ritual: ancient earthwork mounds near Purén served ceremonies, and canoes, wampus, appear in funerals and in stories about death. Some of the Mapuche world view may be shared with the peoples of the central Andes, perhaps through the migrations after Tiwanaku. Memory itself is part of Mapuche tradition: the remembered history of independence and resistance since 1540, and of the treaties of the 1870s, often very local, remains a significant part of their culture.

Crafts at Mehrgarh grew steadily more skilled. Period I ornaments were made of sea shell, limestone, turquoise, lapis lazuli and sandstone, and there were simple figurines of women and animals. In Period II glazed faience beads were produced and terracotta figurines became more detailed, the women painted and shown with varied hairstyles and ornaments. The first button seals, made of terracotta and bone with geometric designs, also date from this time.

Pottery begins in Period II. In Period III finds become far more abundant as the potter’s wheel is introduced, with more complex designs and animal motifs. Togau ware appears at the start of Period III: first defined by Beatrice de Cardi in 1948 and named after a mound near Kalat, it is decorated with geometric designs, was already made on the wheel, and is found widely in Balochistan and eastern Afghanistan, at 84 sites according to Possehl. Pipal-leaf designs are used from Period VI, and sophisticated firing techniques in Periods VI and VII. By Period VIII the quality of the designs seems to have suffered from mass production and a growing interest in bronze and copper vessels.

Metalworking began early. A few copper items date from Period IIB, and the technologies of Periods II and III included stone and copper drills, updraft kilns, large pit kilns and crucibles for melting copper; residents made tools from local copper ore. A wheel-shaped copper amulet about 6,000 years old is the oldest known example of the lost-wax technique. It was made of unalloyed copper, an unusual innovation that was later abandoned.

The objects of the Sanxingdui pits had been broken, perhaps ritually disfigured, then burned and carefully buried. Without written records, what they meant has to be inferred from the objects themselves, and several interpretations have been offered. Eye-shaped objects were also found, which may suggest a worship of eyes. According to the French sinologist Corinne Debaine-Francfort, the paint on the bronze faces, black on the eyes and eyebrows and vermilion on the lips, nostrils and ear holes, is evidence of rituals very different from those of the Shang: she reads the vermilion as something offered for the head to taste, smell and hear, or as giving it the power to breathe, hear and speak. Archaeologists believe the heads were mounted on wooden supports or totems, perhaps dressed in clothing.

Liu Yang concludes that masked ritual was central to the community life of Sanxingdui, and suggests that the masks may have been worn by a shi, the “personator” of early Chinese ritual: usually a close young relative who stood for a dead ancestor to whom sacrifice was offered. On this view the masked figures impersonated supernatural beings in order to bring about some communal good. Another scholar compares the bulging-eyed heads with the “eye-idols” of Julian Jaynes’s bicameral mentality hypothesis.

Some see a picture of the cosmos in the finds. Birds, dragons, snakes and tigers predominate, and since East Asians had long linked four animals with the four quarters of the sky (the Azure Dragon, the Vermilion Bird, the White Tiger and the Black Tortoise), the bronzes might represent the universe, though whether they served to communicate with spirits is unclear. The bronze tree has been identified by some with the Fusang tree of Chinese mythology, and the many fish- and bird-shaped objects have been suggested as totems of the legendary Shu rulers Boguan and Yufu, whose name means “fish cormorant”.
Classic Thule life centred on bowhead whales, hunted by cooperating boat crews under a captain, the umialik, and used for food, fuel, house frames and tools.

The Yangshao left no texts, so their beliefs have to be inferred from burials, buildings and images. A common custom was to place dead children in pottery urns and bury them near the foundations of houses; all the children found buried in this way were girls. Burials are also central to the long debate on how Yangshao families were organised, since the different views rest on different readings of the graves.

Large buildings excavated at several Yangshao sites appear to have served as public ritual spaces rather than homes for an elite; substantial palace-like houses for elites appear only later, in the late Longshan culture at sites such as Guchengzhai and Taosi. Feasting mattered too. Archaeological research indicates that brewing beer and communal feasting were integral to Yangshao culture: the beer was made mainly from common millet and rice, never, it seems, from foxtail millet, which suggests that rice may have been a valued resource in the larger settlements. The narrow-necked jiandiping amphorae may have been used to ferment grain, or, as other research suggests, to filter the drink.

The Yangshao also left images. A dragon figure dating to the fifth millennium BCE is the world’s oldest known depiction of a dragon. Painted pottery shows human faces and animals, especially fish in the early period. At Banpo and Jiangzhai, marks incised on pottery have been read by a few scholars as numerals or as forerunners of Chinese characters, but these readings are not widely accepted.

The layers at the Hougang site show the Yangshao followed by the Longshan and then the Shang cultures, and the Yangshao is understood to have turned into the cultures that came after it in the region. Its painted pottery tradition continued westward in the Majiayao culture. Its mixed farming, spreading across more and more sites, moved people away from gathering and became the basis of an agricultural society in the Central Plain.

Yangshao times saw settlement hierarchies, large public buildings, the first rammed-earth wall in China, the first walled town of the Yellow River valley, signs of an early chiefdom at Xipo, the possible beginnings of sericulture and the oldest known depiction of a dragon. Palace-like houses for an elite, and a clearer separation of classes, followed only in the late Longshan culture.

Today the Yangshao site in Mianchi County, Sanmenxia, which gave the culture its name, has a museum next to the excavations.

Lebanon's weight has always exceeded its size. Beirut's banks served the Gulf Arabs, its port and merchants supplied the region, and its culture, carried by a diaspora larger than the home population, with Brazil's 5–7 million the largest community, is known across the Arab world and beyond. The French Mandate left a francophone country: almost 40% of Lebanese speak French and 70% of secondary schools teach in it, and Lebanon hosted the Francophonie Summit in 2002 and the Jeux de la Francophonie in 2009. It is a founding member of the United Nations and the Arab League, held an Arab League summit in 2002, concluded an association agreement with the European Union in 2001 and sits in the Non-Aligned Movement, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation and the Group of 77.

Its wars have shaped the region. Some 100,000 Palestinians fled to Lebanon in 1948 and their descendants, 174,000 to 450,000, still live there, half in camps and barred from many occupations; their militias drew Israel's invasions of 1978 and 1982 and the United Nations' UNIFIL force. Syria occupied the country from 1976 to 2005, Israel from 1985 to 2000, and the Taif Agreement of 1989, brokered by a Saudi–Moroccan–Algerian committee, became the template for its sectarian peace. Hezbollah, armed by Iran, made Lebanon the front line of the Israel–Iran rivalry. Saudi Arabia pledged $1.5 billion and the European Union about $1 billion to rebuild the country after the 2006 war.

The land east of the Uruguay River was inhabited for 13,000 years by hunter-gatherers, and at the Spanish arrival in 1515 by some 9,000 Charrúa, 6,000 Chaná and a few Guaraní. Spain founded Soriano in 1624, Portugal a fort at Colonia del Sacramento in 1680, and Spain Montevideo in 1726 as a stronghold whose harbour soon rivalled Buenos Aires. In 1811 José Gervasio Artigas rose against Spain and won the Battle of Las Piedras on 18 May; championing federalism against the centralism of Buenos Aires, he took Montevideo in 1815 and organised the Federal League of six provinces. In 1816 10,000 Portuguese troops invaded from Brazil and after four years annexed the Banda Oriental as the province of Cisplatina.

On 25 August 1825 the Thirty-Three Orientals under Juan Antonio Lavalleja declared independence with the backing of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, and the 500-day Cisplatine War followed between Brazil and the United Provinces. Neither won, and in 1828 the Treaty of Montevideo, promoted by the United Kingdom through Viscount John Ponsonby, created Uruguay as an independent state; its first constitution was adopted on 18 July 1830. The new country had just under 75,000 people and two parties, the Blancos of the second president, Manuel Oribe and the Colorados of the first, Fructuoso Rivera, whose quarrel became the Guerra Grande in 1839.

The empire was a tribal state held together by its founder's management of Pashtun alliances and by the plunder of India. Ahmad Shah's eight invasions brought Kashmir and most of the Punjab under Afghan rule, with Lahore governed by Afghans, and the sack of Delhi in 1757 yielded the booty he coveted; the Mughal emperor was left in nominal control of his city as long as he acknowledged Afghan suzerainty south of the Indus up to the Sutlej. Ahmad was credited with balancing tribal alliances and hostilities to a high degree and with directing tribal energies away from rebellion. That balance was later upset by his grandson Zaman Shah, who replaced Barakzai leaders with men of his own Sadozai lineage.

The empire's reach was fixed by negotiation as much as conquest. Rebellions in the north around Bukhara led Ahmad Shah and the Uzbek Emir of Bukhara to agree that the Amu Darya would divide their lands, and he may have sought a similar sphere of influence with the Qing, as he had with the Ottomans, who divided Iran with him. In 1763 he occupied the lands between Tashkent and Kokand at the plea of Fazil Biy of Kokand and Kyrgyz chieftains against Qing expansion, withdrawing by 1764 when no alliance formed, and sent an embassy to Beijing with a letter, probably a fath-nama celebrating Panipat, and gifts of four horses, painted by the Qing court painter Giuseppe Castiglione.

The empire began to unravel before its founder died. From 1762 his hold loosened: parts of the Punjab were lost to the Sikhs, and northern territories to the Uzbeks, forcing the compromise on the Amu Darya. Ahmad Shah died in the mountains east of Kandahar in 1772. His successors governed so ineptly amid serious unrest that within fifty years the empire as such was at an end and Afghanistan was in civil war. The quarrels among Timur Shah's sons after 1793 gave outside powers their pretext to intervene; Zaman Shah's purge of Barakzai chiefs brought his overthrow and blinding in 1801, and Ranjit Singh, who had wrested power from Zaman's forces in Punjab, gave him asylum.

Zaman's fall opened a period of even greater violence: Mahmud Shah's first reign lasted two years before Shuja Shah replaced him; Shuja's treaty with the East India Company in June 1809 was followed within weeks by his deposition; Mahmud's second reign ended when his brother deposed him in 1818; Sultan Ali Shah was strangled by his brother Isma'il, and the Durranis lost Kashmir to the Sikh Empire at the Battle of Shopian in 1819. By 1818 the Sadozai controlled little more than Kabul and the territory within 160 kilometres of it, having alienated the other Durrani lineages. Ayub Shah was deposed and presumably killed in 1823, and Dost Muhammad Khan and the Barakzai dynasty deposed the Sadozai in Kabul, superseding the empire with the Emirate of Afghanistan. A Sadozai line held Herat until 1863.

Lagash left records of a kind few early Sumerian cities match. The Stele of the Vultures is among the earliest depictions of an organised battle, and the Gudea cylinders found at Girsu contain the longest known text in the Sumerian language. The First Dynasty, though left off the Sumerian King List, exercised considerable influence in the region in the time before the dynasty of Akkad, and the prologue of the Code of Ur-Nammu boasts 'He slew Nam-ha-ni the ensi of Lagash', a measure of how much the city still counted.

Its reach was felt in its neighbours. Eannatum's conquests ran from Elam and Urua in the east to Kish, Akshak and Mari, and Ur remained under Lagashite kings even as their power waned, until Lugalkinishedudu of Uruk claimed it; after Akkad's fall Ur-Baba's son Enannipadda and Gudea's building works show Lagash again dominant at Ur. Some researchers now hold that Gudea's reign overlapped Ur-Nammu's rather than falling well before it in a time of Gutian power, since Ur-Baba's appointment of a high priestess at Ur fell between those of Naram-Sin and Ur-Nammu. The site itself, roughly 3.5 by 1.5 km and one of the largest in the region, was first dug for six weeks by Robert Koldewey in 1887, who took it for an extended burial place; Thorkild Jacobsen and Fuad Safar found the first evidence of its identification as Lagash in 1953, and excavation resumed in 2019 under Holly Pittman of the Penn Museum.

Sidon's power lay on the water, and its history is one of conquerors. Throughout antiquity it fell in turn to Assyrians, Babylonians, Egyptians, Persians, Greeks and Romans; its position on a promontory with two harbours did not save it from Nebuchadnezzar II, who made it part of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, nor from the Achaemenid Empire, which took the Phoenician cities in the 6th century BCE. In the Amarna age, around 1350 BCE, the Lebanese coastal city-states fought for dominance as Egypt declined: the Akkar Plain rebelled with Hittite support to become the kingdom of Amurru, the Mitanni Empire that had dominated Syria fell apart under the campaigns of Suppiluliuma I of Hatti, and Tutankhamun and his general Horemheb scrambled to keep Egypt's hold on the southern Levant.

The Sidonian fleet was the city's chief contribution to its overlords' wars. At the Battle of Salamis in 480 BCE its navy fought on the Persian side against the Greeks, and from the middle of the 5th century BCE warships were stamped on its coins. Such service had its reward: for supporting Cambyses II's conquest of Egypt the Persian king granted Sidon Dor, Joppa and the Plain of Sharon. At the end of the Persian era, in 351 BCE, Artaxerxes III invaded Phoenicia, and in 333 BCE Alexander the Great occupied the city.

Sidon was a kingdom under its own kings for most of its ancient history, whatever empire stood over it. In the Amarna period its ruler Zimredda answered to Egypt; under the Achaemenids a Sidonian king still reigned, and the sarcophagus of Eshmunazar II, probably of the 5th century BCE, shows kingship and the priesthood of Ashtart joined in one family. Persian influence was strong and can be seen in the changed architectural style of the city; under the Persians Sidon eclipsed Tyre to become the paramount city in Phoenicia, and Cambyses II enlarged its territory with Dor, Joppa and the Plain of Sharon. Under Alexander's successors it enjoyed relative autonomy.

The Hellenistic necropolis has yielded the Alexander Sarcophagus, likely the tomb of King Abdalonymus rather than of Alexander, the Lycian tomb and the Sarcophagus of the Crying Women, all now in the Archaeological Museum of Istanbul. Under Roman domination the city kept minting its own silver coins; Herod, king of Judaea, built it a theatre, and in the reign of Elagabalus it became a Roman colony, renamed Colonia Aurelia Pia Sidon in honour of its imperial sponsor. The Hebrew Bible, which calls Sidon the mother city of Tyre and says the Sidonians long oppressed Israel, records Solomon's marriage alliance with the Sidonians and names Jezebel a daughter of King Ithobaal I of Sidon. In Byzantine times, after the earthquake of 551 CE, the law school of Berytus took refuge in the city.
Glass and purple dye were Sidon's two chief industries; a considerable mound of broken Murex trunculus shells near the southern harbour shows the scale of the dye works.

Artaxata was laid out at the junction of trade routes connecting the Greek world with Bactria, India and the Black Sea, and the Armenians prospered on that traffic. Its position in the Araks valley on the Silk Road soon made it a centre of bustling economic activity and international trade, linking Persia and Mesopotamia with the Caucasus and Asia Minor; the bathhouses, markets, workshops and administrative buildings that sprang up in the reign of Artashes I show its wealth, and the city had its own treasury and customs. The remains of the huge walls that Artashes built can still be found, and an amphitheatre was added under Artavasdes II (55–34 BCE).

Tigranes the Great founded Tigranakert in the 1st century BCE as a new capital more central to his expanding empire; it had 120,000 people, many temples and an amphitheatre. Josephus describes Tigranes' marching host with its camels, donkeys and mules for baggage, its sheep, cattle and goats for food and its hoards of gold and silver, 'like locusts or the dust of the earth', though the numbers Israelite historians gave were probably exaggerated. Horses had been the pride of the Armenian warrior since ancient times, and Sallust called the cavalry 'remarkable by the beauty of their horses and armor'. The kingdom's traditional fifteen provinces never all existed at once; in reality it comprised nearly 200 districts of varying size and type.

The Marinids remade the religious and intellectual life of Morocco. They pioneered the madrasa there, a type of institution born in north-eastern Iran by the early 11th century that had been antithetical to Almohad doctrine: the Saffarin Madrasa of Fez in 1271 was the first, the al-Attarine followed in 1323, and the Bou Inania, the largest, was also a Friday mosque, with others from Salé and Meknes to Taza, Tlemcen and Marrakesh. The Qarawiyyin reached its apogee in prestige and scope, and the age produced fiqh, poetry, science, geography and above all history, in part because the dynasty wanted histories to legitimise it. Ibn Khaldun was the most famous figure of this intellectual life, shared with Nasrid Granada, and Ibn Battuta set out on his 29-year journey in 1325.

In architecture the Marinids refined the Almoravid and Almohad legacy with ever more elaborate wood and stucco and were the first to use zellij mosaic tilework extensively, which became standard in Moroccan building; their style was closely akin to the Nasrid Alhambra. Their madrasas in Fez, Salé and Meknes are counted among the greatest works of western Islamic architecture of the period, beside the Grand Mosque of Fes el-Jdid (1276), the Great Mosque of Taza (1294) and the Chellah necropolis gate of 1339. The growing weight of sharifian families and the popular veneration of the Idrisids under their rule prepared the way for the Saadians and Alawis.

The army was divided between the companion cavalry, the hetairoi, and the foot companions, the pezhetairoi, who may have existed since the reign of Alexander I, with allied troops, foreign levies and mercenaries. The cavalry, noblemen in muscled cuirasses, became well known in Greece during the Peloponnesian War; the infantry were poorly trained shepherds and farmers. Nicholas Viktor Sekunda puts the army at 10,000 infantry and 600 cavalry when Philip II acceded in 359 BCE.

Philip II made this levy a professional force. He introduced the Macedonian phalanx armed with the long sarissa pike, gave the infantry peltai shields, helmets, greaves and cuirasses or kotthybos stomach bands, formed the elite hypaspistai and the royal bodyguards, the somatophylakes, adopted the Scythian flying-wedge cavalry formation, hired Cretan archers and Thracian, Paeonian and Illyrian javelin throwers and slingers, and employed engineers to build siege engines and bolt-firing artillery. The mines of Crenides, refounded as Philippi in 356 BCE, paid for a permanent standing army and the kingdom's first small navy of triremes. This army beat the Illyrians and Paeonians, took Amphipolis, Pydna and Potidaea in 357–356 BCE, crushed Onomarchus at the Battle of Crocus Field in 352 BCE, destroyed Olynthos in 348 BCE and, after failed sieges of Perinthus and Byzantion in 340 BCE, defeated Athens and Thebes at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE.

Great Moravia's name has lasted chiefly through letters. Constantine, later Saint Cyril, devised the Glagolitic alphabet, the first dedicated to a Slavic language, and with Methodius translated the Gospel and then, in Methodius's words, “all the Scriptures in full, save Maccabees” into Old Church Slavonic, which became the fourth liturgical language of Christendom. Though the Slavic liturgy lasted only about 22 years in Moravia, the disciples expelled in 886 carried it to Bulgaria, Croatia and Bohemia; at the Preslav Literary School Bulgarian disciples such as Naum and Clement of Ohrid created the Cyrillic alphabet, which became the script of the Bulgarian Empire and Kievan Rus', and Old Church Slavonic remains the liturgical language of several Orthodox churches.

Moravia's churches, more than 25 identified in the core lands, ranged from three-nave basilicas at Mikulčice and Bratislava to rotundas; its granulated earrings and gilded buttons formed a recognisable jewellery style. Politically it was the first West Slavic state and reached early feudalism, the social basis of the later medieval kingdoms of the region. In the nineteenth century Great Moravia became a theme of Czech and Slovak romantic nationalism, in the twentieth it served a Czechoslovak identity, and it is named in the preamble of Slovakia's constitution; the double cross thought to have come with Cyril and Methodius is in Slovakia's arms.

Very little is known of the Indo-Greek economy, though it appears to have been active. The abundance of the coinage suggests large mining operations, particularly in the Hindu Kush, and an important monetary economy; the kings struck bilingual coins in both the Greek round standard and the Indian square standard, so money seems to have circulated through every part of society, and the Kunindas to the east and the Satavahanas to the south adopted Indo-Greek monetary conventions, which points to extensive cross-border trade. The coinage is counted among the most artistically brilliant of antiquity.

Trade ran in every direction. Zhang Qian, visiting Bactria about 128 BCE, found bamboo canes from Qiong and cloth from Shu in its markets and was told that merchants bought them in Shendu, northwestern India, a settled farming land like Bactria. Across the Indian Ocean the Ptolemies had built the Red Sea ports of Myos Hormos and Berenike for voyages to the Indus delta, Kathiawar and Muziris; Eudoxus of Cyzicus sailed to India about 130 BCE and returned with perfumes and gemstones, and by the time Indo-Greek rule was ending up to 120 ships a year left Myos Hormos for India. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea records old drachmas of Apollodotus and Menander still current at Barygaza. Yavana donors funded Buddhist caves at Karla, Nasik and Junnar, and Nasik's grapes were probably first brought by the Greeks.

Southern Rhodesia had grown into one of the most industrialised economies in sub-Saharan Africa. Chromium and manganese, tobacco farming and an immigrant workforce supported a manufacturing sector and iron and steel industries; in 1951 over 90% of white Southern Rhodesians were in occupations the British government classed as skilled. The post-war boom drew about 200,000 white immigrants between 1945 and 1970, raising the white population to 307,000. The economy still rested narrowly on a few primary products, and in 1976 the country held 270,000 whites and six million black Africans.

In December 1966 the United Nations made its sanctions mandatory, barring purchases of Rhodesian tobacco, chromium, copper, asbestos, sugar and beef. Incentives for domestic production expanded industrial output, and companies evaded the embargo through subsidiaries and a clandestine trade network: West Germany remained the largest Western European trading partner until 1973, Japan the chief market outside Africa, Iran supplied oil, Portugal re-exported goods through Mozambique with false certificates of origin, and the Byrd Amendment of 1971 let American firms import chromium and nickel. Rhodesia was a racially segregated society with separate schools for African and non-African children; only the University of Rhodesia was not segregated. White settlement was transient: between 1955 and 1979 the country took in 255,692 white immigrants and lost 246,583.

Ife is the holy city of the Yoruba and the source of their royal lines. By its traditions the dynasties of Ila Orangun, Owu, Ketu, Sabe, Egba, Popo, Ijesha and Oyo descend from Oduduwa, and through Oranmiyan's son Eweka the second dynasty of Benin as well; Oyo became one of the most powerful of Africa's medieval states, and Benin a major empire. The Ooni is regarded as chief priest and custodian of the holy city of all the Yoruba, and since the Yoruba Orisha Congress of 1986 he has held an international standing the title had not had since the city's colonisation by the British.

Ife's art is what the world chiefly knows of it. Its naturalistic bronze, stone and terracotta sculptures, which reached their peak between 1200 and 1400, are significant examples of naturalism in pre-colonial African art, distinguished by their regalia, facial marking patterns and body proportions; the life-size copper mask of King Obalufon II, honoured as the Yoruba patron deity of brass casting, weaving and regalia, is the best documented. Its glass beads travelled farther still, to Igbo-Ukwu, to Gao and Essouk in Mali, to Kissi in Burkina Faso, to Mauritania and Ghana, as a currency of power and belief for Yoruba, West Africans and, in time, the African diaspora. The city is now home to the Obafemi Awolowo University and Oduduwa University, and remains, as the city of 401 deities, the place where the orisha are celebrated through the year.

The republic's history is the history of Cuba's dependence on the United States and of the resistance it bred. The Platt Amendment made the island the model of a client state, and the Treaty of Relations of 1934 replaced the right of intervention with economic obligation, a guaranteed share of the American sugar market in exchange for preferential treatment of American business. By world standards Cuba in 1958 was relatively well advanced, with Latin America's highest ratio of hospital beds to people and a middle class comparable to that of the United States, and it was a member of the League of Nations and the United Nations.

Its labour movement stood out in Latin America. The general strike of 1930, a long series of militant stoppages and the first national union of sugarcane workers made Cuban labour by 1933 more highly organised and more radically led than almost any proletariat in Latin America, and the unions later won perhaps the largest privileges in the region, including bans on dismissals and mechanisation, at the cost of the unemployed and the peasants. The World Bank's finding in 1951 that 80 to 90 per cent of rural children had intestinal parasites, a 1959 survey showing 72 per cent of the population afflicted, chronic unemployment of 25 per cent and a bottom fifth taking 2 per cent of income, the lowest share recorded anywhere, are the measure of the inequality against which the revolution of 1959 was made.

The republic's economy rested on farming and on slavery, which was central to the Texian economy, above all in agriculture. Its main exports were crops, chiefly cotton and corn; it imported iron, machinery and goods such as tea, beer and chocolate from the nations that recognised it, and small amounts went to Russia and Spain. Settlers from the southern states brought slavery with them; it fuelled the economy and reinforced social inequality. The Constitution of 1836 wrote it into law: African slaves brought to Texas remained slaves and could not be emancipated without the consent of Congress, Congress could make no law restricting slavery or the slave trade, and no free person of African descent, in whole or in part, might reside permanently in the republic without that consent. Texans of Mexican descent were Tejanos, the Anglo-Americans Texians; women worked in domestic labour, agriculture and business with very limited legal rights.

Public finance was weak: there was no central bank, the Texas dollar was volatile and private banking largely unregulated. The cotton price crash of the 1840s bankrupted the republic, and its government's huge debts became a motive for annexation. Congress nevertheless chartered colleges, from the University of San Augustine in 1837 to Baylor University in 1845. In 1839 Texas became the first nation to enact a homestead exemption protecting a person's primary residence from creditors.

Its 1836 constitution entrenched slavery in the state: slaves could not be freed without the consent of Congress, Congress could pass no law against slavery or the slave trade, and no free person of African descent could reside permanently in the republic.

Early San societies left paintings on rock across southern Africa, showing hunting, battles, domestic life and mythological events. A BBC series of 2005 set San paintings made about 200 years ago beside Palaeolithic European paintings 14,000 years old, drawing on David Lewis-Williams’s work on their symbolic meanings, and Richard Wicksteed’s film In God’s Places (1995) follows the San cultural legacy of the southern Drakensberg. The Tsodilo Hills of northern Botswana bear particular witness to the long presence of the San there.

San crafts serve a life on the move: the kaross cloak, the hide sling and smaller bags, the digging stick, ostrich eggshells used as water containers, and bows, arrows and spears for the hunt, with the poison that comes from beetle larvae. Music, sacred dance and storytelling fill much of the time of people of every age, and San languages, rich in click consonants, carry a large body of stories and myths.

The San have also been filmed and written about for more than half a century. John Marshall documented the Juǀʼhoansi of Nyae Nyae from 1951 to 2000, and his sister Elizabeth Marshall Thomas wrote The Harmless People (1959). Jamie Uys’s comedy The Gods Must Be Crazy was made when the ǃKung had recently been forced into sedentary villages, and its San actors were confused by instructions to act out exaggerated versions of a hunting life they had almost abandoned.

More than 400 distinct Aboriginal peoples have been identified, named after their ancestral languages, dialects or ways of speech, from the Yolngu of eastern Arnhem Land and the Arrernte of central Australia to the Noongar of southern Western Australia. Wider names are also used: Koori in New South Wales and Victoria, Murri in Queensland, Anangu in the central deserts, Palawa in Tasmania. Some identify as saltwater, freshwater, rainforest or desert peoples. Harry Lourandos describes three main cultural areas, Northern, Southern and Central; the first two, richer in marine and woodland resources, were more densely populated.

At the time of European colonisation they spoke more than 250 languages, used varying degrees of technology and lived in many kinds of settlement. Each language and its people are connected with a stretch of territory known as Country, with which they have a spiritual connection, and over the millennia law and religion developed alongside complex trade networks and relations between groups. Knowledge of pre-colonial societies still depends largely on outside observers, whose views were filtered through colonial ways of seeing.

Desert peoples such as the Pitjantjatjara have inherited adaptations to cold nights and to fever. Today remote communities on traditionally owned land, of 20 to 300 people, are often closed to outsiders for cultural reasons.

A winter campaign broke the remaining resistance. Crazy Horse surrendered in 1877 and was killed by a soldier later that year; Sitting Bull fled to Canada and surrendered in 1881. In 1877 some bands signed a treaty ceding the Black Hills, whose legitimacy remains disputed. In December 1890 Sitting Bull was killed at Standing Rock by Indian police sent to arrest him, and two weeks later the 7th Cavalry, with Hotchkiss guns, killed at least 270 Lakota of Spotted Elk’s band at Wounded Knee Creek, about 170 of them women and children. The massacre has endured as a defining symbol of US policy toward Native nations.

Today the Lakota live mainly on five reservations in South Dakota, governed by elected tribal councils; in 2010 they numbered over 170,000, about 2,000 of whom spoke Lakȟótiyapi. The tribes refused the $122 million that the Supreme Court awarded for the Black Hills in 1980, as accepting it would end their claim, and by 2011 the sum held for them exceeded $1 billion.

In Canada, nine Dakota and Lakota nations, Wood Mountain among them, received an apology and recognition as Aboriginal peoples in 2024. Lakota activists such as Madonna Thunder Hawk and Chase Iron Eyes fight the removal of Lakota children into South Dakota’s foster care system.

La Tène metalwork in bronze, iron and gold grew technically out of the Hallstatt tradition but developed a style of its own: complex spirals and interlace, inscribed and inlaid, on fine bronze vessels, helmets, shields, horse trappings and elite jewellery, above all the neck rings called torcs and the clasps called fibulae. Elegant, stylised animal and plant forms were joined to the Hallstatt habit of geometric patterning. The Early Style was mostly static and geometric; the Developed Style moved to forms full of movement such as triskeles, among them the serpentine scroll of the Waldalgesheim Style. Many designs were laid out with compasses, and myths appear in highly stylised form. Celebrated pieces include the Basse Yutz Flagons, the gold-covered Agris Helmet, the Battersea Shield and the Great Torc from Snettisham.

Celtic craftsmen are credited with shrunk-on iron tyres, wagons with front-axle steering, roller bearings in wheel hubs and wooden barrels bound with hoops, and the Roman writer Varro credited them with chain mail. Coins, first minted in the late 4th century BCE, carried stylised portraits, abstract symbols and mythological images.

Music is shown by sculptures of lyre players, thought to be Bards, by remains of string instruments and by the great metal horns called carnyxes. Diodorus Siculus wrote that the Bards sang to lyre-like instruments songs of praise or of obloquy.

Hallstatt society was based on farming, but metalworking was well advanced, and by the end of the period long-distance trade had become economically important. Most settlements were small villages. The largest were mostly fortified hilltop sites, often with the workshops of bronze, silver and gold smiths; the greatest, the “princely seats” or Fürstensitze, had elite residences, rich burials, monumental buildings and fortifications, and some have been called “the first cities north of the Alps”. The Heuneburg on the upper Danube, ringed by nine very large grave mounds, is thought to be the Celtic city of Pyrene mentioned by Herodotus; Mont Lassois in eastern France, with the rich grave of Vix at its foot, is another.

Social distinctions grew sharper, with emerging elites of chieftains and warriors. Society is thought to have been tribal, though very little is known of it, and ancient DNA points to matrilineal “dynastic elites”. Hallstatt itself was untypical, its economy resting on salt, mined most intensively from the 8th to the 5th centuries BCE. Some 1,300 burials holding about 2,000 people have been found there, many with goods well above subsistence, and most are now thought to belong not to miners but to a richer class who controlled the mines. No settlement has been found; it may lie under the later village.

Crafts were standardised: spoked-wheel wagons are highly uniform, the potter’s wheel appeared, and buildings in Silesia used a standard unit of length of about 0.785 m.

The later Hallstatt art of the western zone is generally agreed to form the early period of Celtic art. Its decoration is mostly geometric and linear and is best seen on fine metalwork from graves. Animals, waterfowl above all, are often worked into objects, more often than humans, and in the west there are almost no narrative scenes; these traits passed to the La Tène style. Common objects include weapons, in Hallstatt D often with “antenna hilts” ending in curving forks, and jewellery: fibulae with rows of discs hanging on chains, armlets and some torcs, mostly bronze, with gold in the princely burials. A few pieces, the Strettweg Cult Wagon, the Warrior of Hirschlanden and the bronze couch held up by “unicyclists” from the Hochdorf Chieftain’s Grave, are each one of a kind.

The eastern zone has more human figures and some narrative scenes, from Hallstatt C onward, traced to the situla art of northern Italy and the northern Adriatic. The fashion for decorated bronze buckets, situlae, spread north from about 600 to 400 BCE; the Vače situla from Slovenia is an example. Their scenes, mostly of feasts, hunting and war, show life from what Ruth and Vincent Megaw call a masculine viewpoint.

Iron swords became common after about 800 BCE, and steel was made for them. Builders used long saws for great planks, and the Vix palace shows a mastery of geometry and carpentry. Instruments included harps, lyres, zithers, panpipes, horns, drums and rattles.

The Taklamakan Desert in the middle of the Tarim Basin is barren, but meltwater from the surrounding mountains feeds streams that people turned into oases with mild microclimates and intensive farming. From around 2000 BCE these oases supported settled farming communities. Their irrigation technology had first developed in the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex west of the Pamirs, though how it reached the Tarim is unclear, and their staple crops, wheat and barley, also came from the west.

By the 2nd century BCE the settlements had become city-states; the Book of Han lists 36 statelets in the basin. The largest were Kucha, with 81,000 inhabitants, and Agni, with 32,000. Kucha was ruled by royal families, sometimes on their own and sometimes as vassals, with some 30 named posts below the king, all but the highest in pairs of left and right; its kings took the title Ñäktemts soy, the equal of the Kushan “Son of God”. The Book of Jin describes a city with threefold walls, a thousand temples and stupas, and a palace “glittering like an abode of the gods”.

The people grew red millet, wheat, rice, legumes, hemp, grapes and pomegranates, and reared horses, cattle, sheep and camels. They mined metals and minerals in the mountains and made leather goods, fine felts and rugs.

The Longshan culture is noted for its highly polished black pottery, also called egg-shell pottery. Its potters used the wheel and made thin-walled vessels with great skill; the ware spread across North China and is found in the Yangtze valley and as far as the southeastern coast. Already in the Miaodigou II phase tools and pottery were much improved on those of the Yangshao culture, and the quick wheel came into wide use.

Crafts were centred in the large towns. Liangchengzhen and Yaowangcheng in Shandong produced pottery, stone tools and textiles, and there is evidence of fermented drinks and of prestige goods of jade and metal, so they were also regional centres of production and exchange. The late period saw more widespread and skilled making of copper tools, rings and bells, with a few objects of bronze and brass, before the Bronze Age cultures that followed; most scholars place the start of the Chalcolithic in the Longshan of 2600–2000 BCE.

Builders raised town walls of rammed earth and improved the making of wells: the Hougang II variant of northern Henan and southern Hebei has the first wells of the Yellow River area, dug by a method that early Bronze Age states there went on using. Houses of the Sanliqiao II variant were built above ground, sunk partly into it, or dug sideways into loess cliffs, their walls often plastered.

Towards the end of the 3rd millennium BCE the population fell sharply in most of the region and many large centres were abandoned, possibly through environmental change linked to the end of the Holocene Climatic Optimum. In the Wei River valley the Kexingzhuang II sites already show a decline that scholars put down to migration caused by environmental change. The basin of the Yi and Luo rivers in central Henan was the exception: there population and social complexity grew fast, and material culture runs on without a break through a Xinzhai phase to the Erlitou culture. A 70-hectare walled centre at Xinzhai is said to lead “typologically directly to early Erlitou”. At Taosi there is no such continuity, which suggests a collapse there and later expansion from the Erlitou core. In Shandong the Longshan was followed by the Bronze Age Yueshi culture.

The discovery of the Longshan culture mattered to a debate over the origins of Chinese civilisation: J. G. Andersson, who excavated Yangshao in 1921, had traced its painted pottery to the west, a view Chinese researchers questioned. The Longshan’s bronze, its many towns and its thin black pottery made on the quick wheel are taken as signs of growth in production on a new scale, and of a widening gap between rich and poor. Modern Shandong, home of the tall Longshan people, has the tallest people of any Chinese province.

Roman religion was practical and contractual, resting on the principle do ut des, “I give that you might give”. It depended on knowing and correctly performing prayer, rite and sacrifice, not on faith or dogma. Immortal gods ruled heaven and earth, with gods of the underworld and countless lesser deities. Jupiter, the most powerful, stood for the divine authority of Rome’s highest offices. Rome had no native creation myth and matched its deities with the Greek gods, adapting their myths.

Every sacrifice needed a prayer, and the words had to be exact: a mistake could mean starting a whole festival again. Vows promised offerings in return for benefits, and oaths called on the gods as witnesses. The most potent offering was an animal, usually cattle, sheep or pigs, which had to seem willing; its entrails were reserved for the gods and the meat shared in a communal meal. Public rites took place outdoors at an altar within a templum, a space marked out by augury, and the calendars show roughly forty annual festivals.

Neglect of the gods was a kind of atheism, while excessive or fearful devotion was superstitio; either could bring divine anger on the state. Beliefs about an afterlife varied, but care of the dead was among the oldest practices: the departed became one of the di Manes, appeased at the February festival of the Parentalia, and tombs were inscribed Dis Manibus, “to the Manes-gods”.

Christianisation transformed Celtic society. In Ireland the church stamped out animal sacrifice, and Cormac’s Glossary (c. 900) says Saint Patrick banished the rites of the filid that involved offerings to “demons”. Yet the filid lived in easy harmony with the clergy and kept much of their tradition, status and privilege. The sacred marriage of the king with the goddess of sovereignty was purged early from royal inauguration but stayed in literature for centuries.

Much survived in folklore. The scholar Nagy noted that Gaelic oral tradition was very conservative, with tales told in the 19th century almost as in the ancient manuscripts, and mythology based on the old traditions was still common knowledge in Celtic-speaking cultures then; the Celtic Revival collected it. Beltane is still kept, the Puck Fair at Killorglin seems to survive from Lughnasadh, and pilgrimages to holy wells, the clootie wells of Scotland, Ireland and Cornwall, and well dressing in the English Midlands continue. On the Inishkea Islands, Celtic pagan rituals were seemingly performed well into the 19th century.

In the 20th century Celtic paganism became the basis of Celtic neopaganism, from Reconstructionists who try to practise the ancient religion as accurately as possible to eclectic groups, the best known being Neo-Druidry. In Wales the bardic order, revived and codified by the poet and forger Iolo Morganwg, lives on in the eisteddfods.

The central image of every temple was that of Mithras killing a bull, the tauroctony. In Anatolian dress and a Phrygian cap he kneels on the exhausted bull, holds it by the nostrils and stabs it, looking back towards the sun god Sol; a dog and a snake reach for the blood, a scorpion seizes the bull’s genitals, ears of wheat spring from its tail, and the torch-bearers Cautes and Cautopates stand on either side. Other scenes show Mithras born from a rock, striking water from stone, shaking hands with Sol, feasting with him on the bull’s hide and rising to heaven in a chariot. A lion-headed figure entwined by a serpent, perhaps named Arimanius, is generally thought to be linked with time and the seasons.

Initiates swore an oath of secrecy. Most rituals involved feasting, and many seem to have re-enacted episodes of the Mithras narrative, with the senior officers playing Mithras and Sol. Prayers were addressed to the Sun three times a day, and Sunday was especially sacred. Cherry stones point to midsummer festivities; whether Mithras’s birthday fell on 25 December is disputed.

The temples, mithraea, were small, windowless and underground, representing the cave of the bull-slaying, often near springs, with benches for 15 to 30 diners. Porphyry reports moral demands on initiates of the Lion grade, and Julian speaks of “commandments of Mithras”, but doctrine may have varied from place to place, with no central authority.

Cook’s arrival in 1778 began a new phase for Hawaiian. Over the next forty years Spanish, Russian, French and German arrived with explorers and merchants, and Hawaiians who took jobs on their ships carried the language abroad. One of them, the teenage ʻŌpūkahaʻia, known as Obookiah, reached New England, studied at the Foreign Mission School in Cornwall, Connecticut, inspired the mission to Hawaiʻi and told the missionaries about the language before they sailed in 1819.

Under the kingdom Hawaiian was a written national language. Literacy spread so fast that the minister of Public Instruction, Richard Armstrong, stated in his report for 1853 that 75% of adults could read, and the use of the language may have peaked around 1881. Yet native speakers declined from the 1830s to the 1950s, and as early as 1854 some feared it was “soon destined to extinction”. Native Hawaiians were becoming a minority in their own land as foreign labourers arrived: pure Hawaiian students made up 56% of school enrolment in 1890, 32% in 1900 and 16.9% in 1910. Mixed households, where Hawaiian had low prestige, adopted English, and children of many mother tongues spoke English, or Pidgin, together; within a generation it was the main language of all children.

In 2001 native speakers were less than 0.1% of the state’s people. English has largely displaced Hawaiian on six of the seven inhabited islands, and Hawaiian Pidgin is more spoken than Hawaiian; only on Niʻihau, off Kauaʻi, is it still the language of daily life.

Calls for reform within the Catholic Church were old. From the 14th to the 16th century a spiritual revival grew from the preaching friars, lay movements such as the devotio moderna, printing and Christian humanism, and councils with reforming agendas met at Constance in 1415, at Basel, Ferrara and Florence, and at the Fifth Council of the Lateran (1512–1517). Yet papal nepotism and bishops’ wealth, absence from their dioceses and preoccupation with secular power resisted serious reform for centuries, and radical reformers such as Savonarola rose against them.

The worldly excesses of the Renaissance Church, as in the era of Alexander VI (1492–1503), intensified under Pope Leo X (1513–1521), whose use of indulgences to raise funds for Saint Peter’s Basilica was a key impetus for Martin Luther’s 95 Theses. Protestants decisively broke with the Catholic Church in the 1520s. Many rural priests were poorly educated and knew no Latin, and a growing divide separated clergy from laity.

Reform had already begun. From 1514 the Oratory of Divine Love in Rome drew priests and laymen to anonymous charity and talk of reform, and its members became key players in the Church’s answer to the Reformation; new congregations of clergy followed, from the Theatines in 1524. The French historian Henri Daniel-Rops argued that this renewal’s origins were much older than Luther and that it obeyed the Church’s own tradition rather than answering the reformers.

The survival of Solidarity had no precedent in Poland or in the whole Eastern Bloc, a break in the hard-line stance of the ruling party and of the Soviet government. In the elections of 4 June 1989, the first free elections in any Soviet bloc country, the opposition could field candidates against the Communist party for all 100 seats of a new Senate and for one-third of the seats of the Sejm. Solidarity won 99 of the 100 Senate seats and all 161 contestable seats in the Sejm.

The result brought the first noncommunist Prime Minister since the 1940s and, in December 1990, Wałęsa’s election as President. It also set off a chain reaction across the Soviet Union’s satellite states, the mostly bloodless Revolutions of 1989, in Polish the Autumn of Nations, which overthrew each Moscow-imposed regime and led in the end to the dissolution of the Soviet Union in the early 1990s.

Foreign help played a part. The CIA transferred around $2 million a year in cash from 1982, about $10 million over five years, always through third parties; the AFL–CIO raised $300,000 from its members and gave material and cash directly, and the National Endowment for Democracy allocated $10 million. Henry Hyde of the House intelligence committee said the United States supplied clandestine newspapers, broadcasting, money and organisational help and advice.

On 16 November 1989 students marched peacefully through Bratislava. The next day, International Students’ Day and the 50th anniversary of the Nazi storming of Prague’s universities, about 15,000 people joined an official march in Prague, then carried on into the centre with anti-Communist slogans. At about 7.30 pm riot police blocked them on Národní Street and attacked. A false story that a student, Martin Šmíd, had been killed, reported by Radio Free Europe, drew hesitant citizens into the protests. Students and theatres went on strike, and on 19 November Civic Forum was founded in Prague and Public Against Violence in Bratislava.

Demonstrations filled Wenceslas Square and spread to every major city. On 21 November Miloš Jakeš declared on television that socialism was the only alternative, and 4,000 members of the People’s Militias were summoned to Prague, then called off; the Minister of Defence promised that the army would never act against the people. On 24 November the whole Presidium, Jakeš included, resigned, and the next day some 800,000 people gathered at Letná.

On 27 November a two-hour general strike, backed by a reported 75% of the population, showed Civic Forum’s power. On 28 November the Communist Party announced that it would give up power, and the provision on its leading role was struck from the Constitution. On 10 December Gustáv Husák swore in the first government in 41 years not dominated by the Communists, and resigned.

Hardly anyone had thought the Communist state could collapse so quickly. Striking students and theatres did not at first seem likely to intimidate a state that could suppress any demonstration, but the mass demonstrations after 17 November brought down the Jakeš leadership, removed the party from its leading role and produced a non-Communist government, and the general strike of 27 November gave Civic Forum the standing to speak for the nation in talks with the state. Outside events were catalysts: the changes in Poland and Hungary and the collapse of the East German regime encouraged Czechs and Slovaks to take to the streets, and Western broadcasters such as Radio Free Europe, Voice of America and the BBC World Service carried uncensored news despite jamming.

Havel was elected President on 29 December 1989, a day after Dubček became speaker of the federal parliament. Within weeks Havel negotiated the removal of about 73,500 Soviet troops, who left within months. Free elections in June 1990 legitimised the new government. In early 1990 the President and his advisers decided to liberalise prices, break up monopolies and privatise the economy; the end of lifelong employment brought unemployment, met with unemployment benefits and a minimum wage. Freedom of religion grew, with renewed ties to the Vatican and Israel.

The origins of the environmental movement in Europe and North America lay in smoke abatement. The great factories of the Industrial Revolution and the immense growth in coal burning brought air pollution on a scale not seen before to industrial centres, and after 1900 industrial chemical discharges added to the load of untreated human waste. In Britain the mitigation of air pollution was the main environmental cause for most of the century from 1850 to 1950.

Ideas came first from the Romantic movement. Early in the 19th century the poet William Wordsworth called the Lake District “a sort of national property in which every man has a right and interest who has an eye to perceive and a heart to enjoy”. Later a “Back-to-Nature” movement, advocated by John Ruskin, William Morris, George Bernard Shaw and Edward Carpenter, opposed consumerism and pollution and reacted against the cramped, polluted industrial towns by idealising rural life; Ruskin imagined a “small piece of English ground” with “no steam engines upon it”.

In the forests of British India conservation took practical form. James Ranald Martin’s reports on the damage done by deforestation and desiccation argued for forest departments, and the conservation ethic that grew up held three principles: that human activity damaged the environment, that there was a civic duty to maintain it for future generations, and that scientific methods should be used to fulfil that duty.

The Qing dynasty fell in 1911, ending imperial rule, but Confucianism kept a deep hold on social and political relations. After the death of President Yuan Shikai in 1916 China was dominated by warlords, and the government in Beijing could do little against foreign influence. In early 1915 the Twenty-One Demands, with which the Ōkuma Shigenobu government sought to extend Japanese power in southern Manchuria, eastern Mongolia and Shandong, became known to the Chinese public and stirred anti-Japanese feeling. In 1918 the leak of the secret Sino-Japanese Joint Defence Agreement signed by Premier Duan Qirui enraged the public and sparked a student protest movement out of which May Fourth grew. The Russian Revolution of 1917 and Korea’s March 1st Movement of 1919, an example of mass resistance to imperialism, further inflamed Chinese nationalism.

China had entered World War I on the side of the Triple Entente in 1917 and sent 140,000 labourers to the Western Front, yet the Treaty of Versailles awarded the rights to the German territories in Shandong, surrendered by Germany after the Siege of Tsingtao in 1914, to Japan. China’s representatives asked for an end to foreign privileges, the cancelling of the Twenty-One Demands and the return of Shandong, but the Western allies paid them little heed. The American failure to follow through on Woodrow Wilson’s ideals of self-determination was seen as a betrayal, and the outcome became known as the Shandong Problem.

The Harlem Renaissance helped lay the foundation for the civil rights movement after World War II, giving the African-American community a spirit of self-determination, a growing sense of black urbanity and black militancy, and a base for the struggles of the 1950s and 1960s. Many Black artists who came to maturity afterwards were inspired by it, and Du Bois’s idea of double consciousness was revived in the Black Pride movement of the early 1970s. Its new appreciation of folk roots and spirituals gave artists a source of material, and it is regarded as formative for African-American art and for its institutionalisation in white-dominated museums and cultural institutions.

Its reach was international: many Francophone Black writers from the African and Caribbean colonies who lived in Paris were influenced by it, and in Paris the dancer Josephine Baker set fashions for Black and white women alike. Later scholarship has widened its picture. Black feminist critics have re-evaluated the work of women whose contributions were overlooked at the time, and Nella Larsen and Jessie Fauset have gained renewed acclaim. Writers have also recovered its queer culture, from the drag balls of the Hamilton Lodge to the blues of the cabarets, though homosexual acts could still lead to arrest; Henry Louis Gates Jr. wrote in 1993 that the Harlem Renaissance “was surely as gay as it was black”.

In Paris Aimé Césaire started the magazine L’Étudiant noir with his fellow students Léopold Senghor and Léon Damas, as well as Gilbert Gratiant, Leonard Sainville, Louis T. Achille, Aristide Maugée and Paulette Nardal. In its third issue, of May–June 1935, Césaire first used the word négritude in its present sense, in his first published work, “Conscience Raciale et Révolution Sociale”, which disavowed assimilation as a strategy of resistance and used nègre as a positive term. Senghor’s first critical theory piece, “What the Black Man Contributes”, followed in 1939.

Two anthologies mattered most. Damas published Poètes d’expression française 1900–1945 in 1946, with an introduction meant as a manifesto; he saw his message as one for the colonised in general and included poets from Indochina and Madagascar. Senghor followed in 1948 with the Anthologie de la nouvelle poésie nègre et malgache de langue française, which took the manifesto’s role, and its preface by Jean-Paul Sartre, “Orphée Noir” (“Black Orpheus”), carried Négritude into the wider intellectual conversation. From 1960 to 1974 the Dakar School of art in Senegal, founded under the paternalism of President Senghor, gave the philosophy visual form, with a School of Fine Arts created to shape it. In the 1960s some Black writers began to criticise the movement as insufficiently militant.

The institutions of the Empire of Japan were built on the Meiji Restoration, and the Meiji Constitution of 1889 remained in place until the Allied occupation after the Second World War. Japan became the first Asian state to modernise on the Western model, replacing the Confucian hierarchical order once dominated by China with one based on modernity, and its pursuit of colonial interests against its neighbours had far-reaching consequences in East Asia. After the First Sino-Japanese War and the Russo-Japanese War the military came to see itself as a growing world power.

The state built a national system of free public schools that taught reading, writing, mathematics and “moral training” in duty to the Emperor, and spread a standard language, hyōjungo, based on the speech of Tokyo’s samurai classes. The changes also destroyed heritage: most Japanese castles were partly or wholly dismantled, tens of thousands of Buddhist images and temples were smashed during the separation of Shintō and Buddhism, shinbutsu bunri, and tens of thousands of old Shinto shrines were closed. The ideal of samurai military spirit lived on in romanticised form and served as propaganda in the Empire’s wars of the early 20th century.

The era lives on in fiction, from Shimazaki Tōson’s novel Before the Dawn to Akira Kurosawa’s film Yojimbo (1961) and Rurouni Kenshin: The Beginning (2021).

Renaissance writers drew on ancient models, and their thought came to be called classical republicanism, or civic humanism. Niccolò Machiavelli’s Discourses on Livy was the period’s key work on republics, though most writers thought republics could succeed only in small, highly urbanised city-states. In the Dutch Republic anti-monarchism grew during the Eighty Years’ War, which began in 1568, and the brothers Johan and Peter de la Court called all monarchies illegitimate tyrannies. In the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, the Rzeczpospolita, republicanism was the ideology not of merchants but of the landed nobility, who wanted a weak king.

In England James Harrington and John Milton were leading republican thinkers of the Commonwealth, and in the early 18th century the “country” party of the commonwealthmen denounced the corruption of the court, a theory that heavily influenced the American colonists. Montesquieu, Voltaire and Rousseau elaborated the social contract, positive law and mixed government. Republicanism, especially Rousseau’s, was central to the French Revolution, and in 1791 the Society of United Irishmen was founded in Belfast and Dublin.

In the early 19th century republicanism helped inspire the independence movements of Spain’s former colonies, where Simón Bolívar and others identified as republicans and Andrés Bello shaped a “republican internationalism”. Giuseppe Mazzini revived the republican idea in Italy, Brazil’s radical liberals founded a Republican Party in 1870, and Spain had two republics, in 1873–1874 and 1931–1939.

Napoleon’s conquests of the German and Italian states around 1800–1806 did much to stimulate demands for national unity, and in the 19th century nationalism became one of the most significant political and social forces in history. Between 1830 and 1870, the historian J. P. T. Bury argued, it inspired great literature and nurtured heroes, unified Germany and Italy, and threatened the multinational Ottoman and Habsburg empires. In Hispanic America an upsurge of nationalism in the 1810s and 1820s, led by the criollos against the peninsulares, cost Spain nearly all its colonies. Greek and Serbian revolts won independence from the Ottoman Empire, while Polish revolts in 1830 and 1863–64 were harshly crushed by Russia, whose own official ideology was “Orthodoxy, Autocracy, and Nationality”.

In Germany Hegelian historians such as Johann Gustav Droysen and Heinrich von Treitschke saw Prussia as the true carrier of the German spirit, and Otto von Bismarck achieved unification through short wars against Denmark, Austria and France. Jewish nationalism, Zionism, answered antisemitism and pogroms with settlement in Palestine from 1882.

Japan’s defeat of Russia in 1905 awakened nationalism across Asia: in China Sun Yat-sen founded the Kuomintang, and the May Fourth Movement of 1919 followed. After the Second World War the forces of nationalism grew much stronger in Africa, and in the 1950s and 1960s the colonies became independent states. Adria Lawrence argues that colonial nationalism was spurred by the colonial powers’ refusal of equal rights to their subjects.

Critics argue that it is often unclear what a nation is, or whether it is a legitimate unit of rule. The philosopher A. C. Grayling calls nations artificial constructs, “their boundaries drawn in the blood of past wars”. Critics call nationalism divisive, since it stresses differences between people, and potentially oppressive, since it can submerge the individual in a national whole and give leaders the means to manipulate the masses. John Etherington argues that it is inherently exclusionary and potentially violent, and Barry Posen that it increases the intensity of war.

In the liberal tradition the historian Lord Acton put the case for “nationalism as insanity” in 1862: it suppresses minorities and places country above moral principle. Since the late 20th century liberals have been divided, with Michael Walzer, Isaiah Berlin, Charles Taylor and David Miller holding that a liberal society needs a stable nation-state. George Orwell distinguished nationalism from patriotism and called it “power-hunger tempered by self-deception”. Bertrand Russell argued that it weakens the individual’s capacity to judge his country’s foreign policy; Albert Einstein called it “an infantile disease … the measles of mankind”.

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels declared in 1848 that “the working men have no country”, though Vladimir Lenin supported self-determination. Feminist critics argue that nationalism justifies sexual control and repression, and Edward Said that nationalist narratives often go hand in hand with racism.

Most new nation-states since 1815 have emerged through decolonisation, and nationalism has been associated with cultural revivals and pride in national achievement as well as with war. Glenda Sluga notes that “the twentieth century, a time of profound disillusionment with nationalism, was also the great age of globalism.” Sport carries it too: Jeff Kingston finds that sports can ignite nationalist passions as strongly as they can unify and generate goodwill.

The rise of globalism in the late 20th century was followed by a rise of nationalism and populism in Europe and North America, as groups such as Germany’s Pegida, France’s National Front and the UK Independence Party called for restrictions on immigration. In 2014 Scotland voted against independence by 55.3 per cent, and in 2016 British voters chose to leave the European Union. Donald Trump ran in 2016 on the slogans “Make America Great Again” and “America First”, and in 2018 declared himself a nationalist. Nationalist sentiment was used in Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014; Hindu nationalism has grown with the Bharatiya Janata Party, ruling India since 2014; and Catalan nationalists have led a renewed independence movement since 2010.

Scholars continue to debate its moral value, its relation to patriotism and its compatibility with cosmopolitanism, and the study of nationalism, from Carlton Hayes’s survey of 1928 to Anderson’s Imagined Communities, has become a field of its own.

The word fell out of use by the 1860s, and by 1888 Marxists used socialism instead. After the October Revolution of 1917 Lenin made socialism a stage between capitalism and communism, and in 1918 the Bolsheviks renamed their party the Communist Party. The Comintern, founded in 1919, carried the Bolshevik model abroad, while council communism, which arose in Germany and the Netherlands in the 1920s, and left communism opposed it.

After Lenin’s death Marxism–Leninism, resting on dialectical materialism, the leading role of the party and a planned economy with industrialisation and collectivisation, became the official ideology of Communist parties; at its height it covered at least a third of the world’s population. Trotskyism, which upheld permanent and world revolution against Stalin’s socialism in one country, founded the Fourth International in 1938. China and the Soviet Union were at sword’s point by 1960, splitting the world movement into two hostile camps, and anti-revisionists such as the Maoists and Enver Hoxha’s followers rejected the Soviet line after Khrushchev.

Governments modelled on the Soviet Union took power with Soviet help in Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Poland, Hungary and Romania after the Second World War; Tito’s Yugoslavia broke with Stalin in 1948, and the Cuban revolutionaries who overthrew Batista in 1959 became Marxist–Leninist. In Western Europe communist parties joined post-war governments and in the 1970s developed Eurocommunism, and since 1957 communists have often won power in the Indian state of Kerala.

The word comes from the Ancient Greek anarkhia, “without a ruler”; early English usages stressed disorder, and factions of the French Revolution called their opponents anarchists. Precursors are found in China and Greece. The Taoist philosophers Zhuang Zhou and Laozi discussed the legitimacy of the state; Socrates insisted on the right of individual freedom of conscience, the Cynics dismissed human law, and the Stoics favoured a society of friendly relations without a state. In the Sasanian Empire Mazdak called for an egalitarian society and the abolition of monarchy and was soon executed by Kavad I.

Modern anarchism emerged from the Enlightenment. The Renaissance and the Reformation had revived anti-authoritarian secularism in Europe, and the revolutions of the 1790s and of 1848 spurred the ideas of what became classical anarchism. During the French Revolution groups such as the Enragés and the sans-culottes voiced anti-state and federalist feeling. In England William Godwin espoused a philosophical anarchism that morally delegitimised the state, and Max Stirner’s thinking led towards individualism.

Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was the first political philosopher to call himself an anarchist and give the word a positive meaning. In What Is Property? (1840) he described his goal as a “third form of society, the synthesis of communism and property”, and his mutualism found fertile soil in France. Historians place the birth of the anarchist movement between Proudhon and the Saint-Imier Congress of 1872.

Anarchists have taken part in several revolutions, most notably the Paris Commune, the Russian Civil War and the Spanish Civil War. In the Russian Revolution they fought the White movement, above all in the Makhnovshchina in Ukraine. Once the Bolshevik government was secure it harshly suppressed them, including during the Kronstadt rebellion, and crushed the anarchist movement in Ukraine as well, while many workers turned to the Communist parties.

In Spain a long anarchist tradition gave the CNT and FAI a central part in the civil war of 1936–39. In answer to the army rebellion, an anarchist-inspired movement of peasants and workers, backed by armed militias, took control of Barcelona and of large areas of rural Spain, where they collectivised the land. The Soviet Union gave some limited help, but as Stalin asserted Soviet control of the Republican government, communists and other leftists fought each other in the May Days, which ended in another defeat of the anarchists at communist hands.

Classical anarchism also had a violent side. A minority practised propaganda of the deed, revolutionary violence meant as the spark of revolution; most attacks came in the late 1870s, early 1880s and 1890s, and some assassination attempts on heads of state succeeded. Many anarchists distanced themselves from these terrorist acts, but infamy came upon the movement, and the United States tried to bar anarchists with the Immigration Act of 1903. Emma Goldman and Errico Malatesta held violence to be a reaction to state violence, a necessary evil.

Maoism grew out of a Chinese intellectual tradition that by the early 20th century was defined by iconoclasm and nationalism. A small but significant part of the old elite of landlords and bureaucrats lost faith in Confucianism, and the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1911 marked the final failure of the Confucian moral order. During the New Culture Movement of 1915–1919 Chen Duxiu’s periodical New Youth called for the “total destruction of the traditions and values of the past”; it strongly influenced the young Mao Zedong, whose first published work appeared in its pages.

Radical anti-imperialism turned into nationalist fervour when the Treaty of Versailles of 1919 transferred former German lands in Shandong to Japan. The May Fourth Movement began with 3,000 students protesting in Beijing, and the Russian Revolution drew the intelligentsia toward Marxism: to become a Marxist was one way to reject both the traditions of China’s past and Western domination of its present.

After the Long March the party was based in the Yan’an Soviet, where from November 1935 Mao produced most of the works later canonised as the Thought of Mao Zedong and won ideological independence from Moscow. His pamphlet Strategic Problems of China’s Revolutionary War (December 1936) held that China’s circumstances demanded a unique application of Marxist theory, the Sinicization of Marxism. In 1945 the party’s 7th congress made Mao Zedong Thought its unified ideology.

After Mao’s death in 1976, Deng Xiaoping began market reforms in 1978 and reduced the role of ideology in policy, separating Mao from Maoism and making clear that Mao was fallible. Matthew Galway writes that the party did not de-Maoize but reassessed Mao’s legacy, stressing his positive contributions while acknowledging his mistakes. The 1981 resolution credited Mao Zedong Thought with national independence, the transformation of China’s social classes, economic self-sufficiency, the expansion of education and health care and China’s leading position in the Third World, and it remains one of the Four Cardinal Principles of the People’s Republic. Xi Jinping, in a speech of 2013, summed it up as seeking truth from facts, the mass line, and national independence and autonomy.

Contemporary Maoists in China criticise the social inequalities created under the party, and some radicals have backed protests and strikes such as the Jasic incident; Bo Xilai’s mass mobilisation with red songs in Chongqing was called neo-Maoist. In the 2020s the growing wealth gap and the 996 working hours have revived Mao’s thought among China’s generation Z, and the government has censored some Maoist posts.

Abroad, the Communist Party of India (Maoist), designated a terrorist organisation in India, the New People’s Army in the Philippines and the TKP/ML in Turkey still wage armed struggles, while the Workers’ Party of Belgium broke formally with its Maoist past in 2008.

The bureaucratic apparatus that Qin built on Legalist lines was adopted by the Han dynasty and continued to shape Chinese statecraft throughout Chinese history. The meritocratic ideas of xing-ming may have contributed to the founding of the imperial examination, and the Qin judge-magistrate who investigated like a detective lived on in early Han theatre.
