The Qing Yongzheng Emperor more or less quoted the Han Feizi’s praise of law as useful for “correcting the faults of the high, rebuking the vices of the low”.

The modern image of the school owes much to chapters 43 and 40 of the Han Feizi, which shaped an early modern view of Shen Buhai as focused on technique, Shen Dao on power and Shang Yang on law. The scholar Hu Shih called Han Fei and Li Si the “greatest statesmen in Chinese history” and champions of progress through conscious human effort, and Feng Youlan read the Legalists as statesmen who understood that needs change with the times. Scholars and commentators have cited Legalism as an influence on the governance of the People’s Republic of China, particularly under Xi Jinping; Sam Crane has called the modern Chinese state “Confucianism on the outside, Legalist on the inside”. Deng Xiaoping’s saying that a cat is a good cat if it can catch rats, whether white or black, has been compared with the Han Feizi.

Atatürk refused to be dogmatic and described his ideology as based on science and reason. Its six principles, symbolized by the Six Arrows, are republicanism, populism, nationalism, laicism, statism and reformism. Together they form a kind of Jacobinism, which Atatürk defined as using political despotism to break down the social despotism that, he believed, the bigotry of the ulema had encouraged among the traditionally minded population. Republicanism replaced the Ottoman dynasty with popular sovereignty and elected government under the law: “Sovereignty belongs to the nation unrestrictedly and unconditionally.” Populism rejected class conflict in favour of class collaboration and national unity.

Laicism, close to French laïcité rather than the passive Anglo-American secularism, sought to banish religion from government and to bring the religious establishment under the state. Nationalism, drawing on Rousseau’s Social Contract, aimed to make a nation state from the remnants of the multi-ethnic Ottoman Empire, defining the Turkish nation as the people who established the Republic and promoting the motto “How happy is the one who says I am a Turk”; it renounced Pan-Turkism as an impossible goal. Statism had the state regulate the economy and invest where private enterprise would not, and reformism held the reforms irreversible, with no return to systems deemed backward.

Kemalism remains the founding ideology of the Republic of Turkey. Its principles stand in the constitution, which since 1982 declares the Republic “loyal to the nationalism of Atatürk”, and its laicism holds that politicians may not claim to protect any religion or sect, a claim that is legal ground for the permanent banning of a party. Article 66 of the constitution carries the Kemalist notion of nationality: every citizen is recognized as a Turk, regardless of ethnicity, belief and gender. By the early 21st century most Kemalists, within the CHP or outside it, still believed in the original six principles, while others criticized its statist tendencies and sought to reduce them.

Scholarly interest in the transnational history of Kemalism has grown, from the interwar Balkans and Egypt to the Jewish community of British-ruled Palestine and the Muslim world further east, though most of that work, written in the countries concerned, views it positively and offers few critical insights. Scholars argue that Kemalism became a transnational political category through the circulations of the post-Ottoman space, carried by government and also by material culture, ideas of gender and scientific debate. Those who view it positively link its secularism to the Enlightenment. It endures in the symbol of the Six Arrows and in the motto “How happy is the one who says I am a Turk”.

Perón’s critics charged him with contempt for opponents, whom he called traitors and foreign agents. The writer Jorge Luis Borges told the Argentine Society of Writers, after Perón became president in 1946, that “dictatorships breed oppression, dictatorships breed servility, dictatorships breed cruelty”. The United States government portrayed Peronism as a “Nazi menace” in its Blue Book of 1946, and Perón’s admiration for Benito Mussolini is well documented. Carlos Fayt called Peronism “an Argentine implementation of Italian fascism”, and Paul Hayes a fascism “distinctively Latin American”.

Most scholars reject the fascist label. Cristian Buchrucker notes that Peronism arose in a time of growth, not crisis, drew on the working class, not the middle classes, lacked territorial expansionism and never made Argentina a one-party state; Robert Crassweller and others argue it was authoritarian but not a dictatorship. Alan Knight argues that, measured against the “infamous decade” before it, Peronism was socially progressive. Seymour Martin Lipset called it, if fascism at all, “a fascism of the left”.

Marxist critics such as Samuel Baily and Ernesto Laclau saw Peronism as resting on new migrant workers without a clear consciousness of their class interests; Miguel Murmis, Juan Carlos Portantiero and Walter Little found instead that the established working class took part fully and was highly homogeneous.

Hammurabi, sixth king of the Amorite First Dynasty of Babylon, ruled from around 1792 to around 1750 BCE (middle chronology). When he inherited the throne of his father Sin-Muballit, Babylon held little local sway and the local hegemon was Rim-Sin of Larsa. Hammurabi waited until Rim-Sin grew old, conquered his territory in one swift campaign, and later betrayed allies in Eshnunna, Elam and Mari to gain their territories, securing Babylonian dominance over the Mesopotamian plain through military prowess, diplomacy and treachery. His letters nonetheless suggest concern for the welfare of his subjects and an interest in law and justice, and in them he often presents himself as his people's shepherd.

The Code stands in an older tradition. Earlier law collections in Sumerian and Akkadian survive, among them the Code of Ur-Nammu of Ur, the Code of Lipit-Ishtar of Isin and the Laws of Eshnunna, and like Hammurabi's they purport to have been written by rulers; statements of other rulers suggest the custom was widespread. Thousands of legal documents also survive from before and during the Old Babylonian period, among them contracts, judicial rulings and reform documents such as that of Urukagina, king of Lagash. Scribes were still copying the Code of Ur-Nammu when Hammurabi produced his own, which suggests the earlier collections influenced the Code as well as resembling it.

Murasaki Shikibu lived at the height of the Fujiwara clan's power, when Fujiwara no Michinaga was the regent in all but name and the most significant political figure of his day; she is believed to have formed the character of Genji partly through her experience of him. The tale was written to entertain the Japanese court of the 11th century, and it may have been written chapter by chapter, as she delivered installments to aristocratic women, the ladies-in-waiting.

In the Heian period monogatari meant prose fiction in the vernacular of the time, thought suitable only for women and children who could not read Chinese, the official language of government and religion. Writing in kanji, the Chinese characters used for more prestigious literature, was a masculine pursuit, and women were generally discreet in using it. Genji is written mostly in kana, specifically hiragana, in a style associated with women's writing, and outside the vocabulary of politics and Buddhism it contains very few Chinese loan words.

Poetry ran through court conversation. Modifying or rephrasing a classic poem to suit the moment was expected behaviour and often carried thinly veiled allusions. The tale's poems are often in the classic tanka form, and because many were well known to its first readers, usually only the first few lines are given, leaving the rest unspoken. Court manners also made it unacceptably familiar to use a person's given name, so almost no character is named.

The poem was widely admired in the centuries immediately after its publication. Boccaccio's Trattatello in laude di Dante, written between 1351 and 1355, gives the earliest known use of the adjective Divina, likely for its weighty subject and elevated style, and the Comedy was among the first works of vernacular literature to receive serious critical attention, which before 1300 had been reserved for religious texts and classical literature. Commentaries began with Iacopo Alighieri in 1322, and line-by-line commentaries have since been written in languages across Europe, the Americas and Asia. Galileo Galilei is known to have lectured on the Inferno.

During the Enlightenment the work largely fell into obscurity, with exceptions: Vittorio Alfieri, Antoine de Rivarol, who translated the Inferno into French, and Giambattista Vico, who began the romantic reappraisal of Dante by setting him beside Homer. In the English-speaking world it was “rediscovered” by William Blake, who illustrated passages of it, and by the Romantic writers of the 19th century.

Its sources have long been argued over. In 1919 the Spanish priest and scholar Miguel Asín Palacios argued that Dante drew on Ibn Arabi and on accounts of Muhammad's night journey, the Isra and Mi'raj, known in Latin as the Liber scalae Machometi; Francesco Gabrieli doubted it for lack of a means of transmission, while Maria Corti speculated that Brunetto Latini could have brought Dante a copy.

The tomb was soon tested. In December 1652 Shah Jahan's son Aurangzeb wrote to his father that the tomb, the mosque and the assembly hall had developed extensive leaks in the previous rainy season. In 1658 Aurangzeb deposed Shah Jahan and put him under house arrest in the nearby Agra Fort, from where he could see the Taj Mahal; on his death in 1666 Aurangzeb buried him beside his wife. The fanciful writings of Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, a European traveller and gem merchant who visited Agra in 1665, gave rise to the long-lived myth of a Black Taj Mahal that Shah Jahan meant to build across the river; excavations in the 1990s showed that the blackened stones offered as its ruins were discoloured white ones.

Personal and emotional responses to the building have consistently eclipsed scholarly appraisals. It became a widely known symbol of love and also of Shah Jahan's wealth and power. The art historian Ebba Koch reads the whole compound as a symbol of earthly life and the afterlife: the white mausoleum and its garden on one side, the red sandstone side meant for worldly markets on the other, each a mirror of the other, with the great gate as the passage between them. Other stories have no support: tales of Shah Jahan mutilating his builders, of Lord William Bentinck planning to auction its marble, and the theories, promoted by Henry George Keene in 1879 and by William Henry Sleeman, that an Italian or a Frenchman designed it.

Ashoka's existence as a historical emperor had almost been forgotten. The Brahmi script of his edicts was soon forgotten too, and his image in Buddhist circles rested on legends such as the Ashokavadana. In the 19th century James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi; he first identified the "Priyadasi" of the inscriptions with a king of Ceylon, until in 1837 George Turnour found a Sri Lankan manuscript, the Dipavamsa, that associated Piyadasi with Ashoka.

He is credited with helping to spread Buddhism across ancient Asia, though epigraphic evidence suggests that in north-western India and the Deccan it spread less through his missions than through merchants, traders, landowners and artisan guilds. He is often credited with the beginning of stone architecture in India, and most later South Asian scripts derive from the Ashokan Brahmi; whether the script was invented in his reign remains unresolved.

Early scholars, building on the traditional accounts, regarded him as primarily a Buddhist monarch; some have questioned this. Thapar writes that he should be seen both as a statesman inheriting and sustaining an empire and as a person with a strong commitment to changing society through the propagation of social ethics. A theory of Christopher I. Beckwith that Ashoka and the Piyadasi of the major edicts were different kings is not accepted by mainstream scholarship. The State Emblem of the Republic of India is an adaptation of the Lion Capital of Ashoka, and his wheel, the Ashoka Chakra, stands at the centre of the national flag.

His disciples and followers organized his teachings into the Analects. Mencius, in the 4th century BCE, stressed the innate goodness of human beings, and Xunzi, in the 3rd, the shaping of morality by tradition and training. After a setback under the Qin, the works attributed to Confucius were made the official imperial philosophy under Emperor Wu of Han and, in 140 BCE, required reading for the civil service examinations, which continued nearly unbroken until the end of imperial China in 1912. In the Song dynasty the teaching was revived as what is now called Neo-Confucianism, whose best-known scholar was Zhu Xi; it held sway in China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam until the 19th century.

Jesuit missionaries first translated the works into European languages in the 16th century; a team of them published several in Paris in 1687, and such works are thought to have mattered to Deists and other thinkers of the Enlightenment. His descendants were honoured with titles: that of Duke Yansheng, first bestowed in 1055, lasted until the Nationalist government abolished it in 1935. The Kong family tree, now in its 83rd generation, has two million known and registered descendants.

Some follow Confucianism in a religious manner, while many argue that it is less a religion than a secular morality. After the attacks of the Maoist era, veneration resumed in the early 1980s with Communist officials in attendance; in Taiwan the memorial ceremony continued without interruption. Modern scholars are cautious about attributing specific assertions to Confucius himself.

Genghis Khan founded the largest contiguous state in world history, which, according to the historian Christopher Atwood, permanently altered the worldview of European, Islamic and East Asian civilizations. His conquests enabled Eurasian trading systems on a scale not seen before, and he reorganised the legal system under a judicial authority headed by Shigi Qutuqu, though he very likely did not codify the body of laws known as the Great Yasa. His division of it into appanages, however, led it to begin splitting in the late 1200s into the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate and the Yuan dynasty, established by his grandson Kublai Khan in 1271.

In post-Mongol Asia descent from him was a source of legitimacy: Timur ruled behind puppet khans of his line. In Mongolia he was deified after Altan Khan's conversion to Tibetan Buddhism in the late 1500s, and in the 19th and early 20th century came to be seen as the national hero. After the Second World War his cult was repressed and celebrations of the 800th anniversary of his birth in 1962 were cancelled after Soviet threats; since the 1990 revolution he has been rehabilitated, and he is generally recognised as the founding father of Mongolia.

Russian historians have portrayed the rule of the Golden Horde as backward and destructive; modern Chinese historiography has generally viewed him positively. In the West he was seen in the 14th century as a just and wise ruler and by the twentieth as a barbarian warlord; recent scholarship views him as a more complex individual.

The Ayyubid dynasty that Saladin founded outlived him by only 57 years, and the Kingdom of Jerusalem persisted until the late 13th century, but 1187 marked a turning point in the Christian military effort in the region. In medieval Europe he was known as a model of kingship and of regal generosity. As early as 1202/03 Walther von der Vogelweide urged the German king to be more like him; Dante placed him among the virtuous non-Christians in limbo, and Boccaccio depicted him favourably. Lessing's play Nathan the Wise (1779) and above all Sir Walter Scott's novel The Talisman (1825) shaped the romantic modern view.

In the Muslim world his reputation had been largely forgotten, eclipsed by more successful figures such as Baybars of Egypt. The visit of the German emperor Wilhelm II to his tomb in 1898, coupled with anti-imperialist sentiment, encouraged the image of Saladin in the Arab world as a hero of the struggle against the West, building on the one created by Scott and other Europeans. With the rise of Arab nationalism in the 20th century his recapture of Palestine became an inspiration for opposition to Zionism, and the Eagle of Saladin became the symbol of revolutionary Egypt and of several other Arab states.

He has been described as the most famous Kurd in history and is a prominent figure in Arab, Turkish and Kurdish culture. Mark Cartwright writes that appreciation of his diplomacy and leadership in both Muslim and Christian sources of his time suggests that he "is indeed worthy of his position as one of the great medieval leaders".

Bolívar is regarded as a hero and a national and cultural icon throughout Latin America, and in the English-speaking world he is known as Latin America's George Washington. Bolivia and the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela bear his name, as do their currencies, the boliviano and the bolívar. His body was interred at Santa Marta in 1830; in 1842 Páez secured its return to Caracas, and in October 1876 it was moved to the National Pantheon of Venezuela.

From 1842 popular opinion of him in Venezuela became overwhelmingly positive and grew into what scholars have described as the "cult of Bolívar", led by successive heads of state. President Hugo Chávez made extensive use of his image and changed the country's official name to the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela. Chávez also claimed that Bolívar had been poisoned; a commission exhumed the remains on 16 July 2010, and its results, made public in 2011, were inconclusive. In Colombia, allegiance or opposition to Bolívar formed the basis of the Conservative and Liberal parties respectively, and in 1974 the insurgent 19th of April Movement stole a sword said to be his from his Bogotá residence.

His writings remain central to his reputation: the Jamaica Letter has been called a "blueprint of Bolívar's political thought" and the Cartagena Manifesto "one of the great documents of Latin American history". He hoped for a federation of Latin American republics, and at Angostura argued for the abolition of slavery. In 1978 UNESCO created the International Simón Bolívar Prize.

The Zhou that Wu proclaimed has traditionally not been regarded as a dynasty in its own right, since it began and ended with her; it is seen as a brief interruption of the Li family's Tang dynasty. Her fifteen years as emperor were the culmination of nearly half a century of de facto and de jure rule, part of the High Tang period, a peak of China's political power and cultural influence. Her repression of the old aristocracy of Guanzhong and her promotion, often through the examinations, of talented men from less privileged families made social changes that historians are still evaluating, and her ability to select capable officials was admired for the rest of the Tang dynasty and in later dynasties.

In the early Tang, when the emperors were her direct descendants, she was evaluated favourably; later commentary, especially Sima Guang's Zizhi Tongjian, criticised her harshly, and by the Southern Song, when Neo-Confucianism was established as the mainstream political ideology, it determined the evaluation of her. In the 20th century Mao Zedong's wife Jiang Qing rehabilitated Wu as part of a propaganda campaign to suggest herself as his successor.

Modern authors differ. One calls her politically astute and an excellent judge of men, whose rise to power was "steeped in blood"; another holds that the period of her ascendancy was a good one for China, with sound government; a third notes that her murderous and illicit methods encouraged overstaffing and many kinds of corruption. She remains the only woman to have reigned over China as emperor.

At the Leipzig disputation of 1519 Luther asserted that neither popes nor church councils were infallible. In 1520 he published To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church and On the Freedom of a Christian, and on 10 December he publicly burned the bull Exsurge Domine, which required him to recant 41 sentences. Pope Leo X excommunicated him on 3 January 1521. Before the Diet of Worms in April he refused to recant: "my conscience is captive to the Word of God". The Edict of Worms of 25 May 1521 declared him an outlaw.

Frederick III, Elector of Saxony, had him taken in a staged rescue to the Wartburg Castle, where he translated the New Testament from Greek into German; it was published in 1522, and the whole Bible followed in 1534. Written in the German of the Saxon chancellery, intelligible to northern and southern Germans alike, it encouraged a standard version of the language. Returning to Wittenberg on 6 March 1522, he preached the eight Invocavit Sermons, urging trust in God's word rather than violence to bring about change.

From 1525 to 1529 he organised a new church in the Electorate of Saxony with Elector John the Steadfast: a supervisory body, a German Mass published in 1526 with congregational singing and communion in both bread and wine, and in 1529 the Large and Small Catechisms. He wrote hymns such as "Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott". On 13 June 1525 he married Katharina von Bora, a former nun, which set the seal of approval on clerical marriage; she bore six children.

The title he invented was used by monarchs in China and other countries for two millennia, and the sinologist Michael Loewe writes that few would contest that the achievements of his reign “exercised a paramount influence on the whole of China's subsequent history, marking the start of an epoch that closed in 1911”. His main tomb has not been opened; probes have found mercury at some 100 times the natural rate, which lends credit to parts of Sima Qian's description of rivers of mercury.

His reputation has been repeatedly revised. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when some came to see Confucian tradition as an impediment to China, the Kuomintang historian Xiao Yishan stressed his repulse of the northern peoples, and in 1941 Ma Feibai's biography called him “one of the great heroes of Chinese history” and compared him with Chiang Kai-shek. After 1949 a Marxist critique, set out in the Complete History of China of 1955, held that unification had served the ruling group and the merchant class and that the dynasty's fall showed the class struggle.

Mao Zedong, compared with the First Emperor for his persecution of intellectuals, reportedly boasted in 1958 that he had surpassed him “a hundredfold”. From 1972 an official view presented the emperor as a far-sighted ruler who destroyed the forces of division, and a 1974 article in Red Flag blamed the fall of Qin on the lack of thoroughness of his “dictatorship over the reactionaries”. Since the mid-20th century scholars have questioned the image of the tyrant and strict Legalist.

Strengthened by the defeat of Elam, Hammurabi launched a lightning war against Rim-Sin with the help of Zimri-Lim, citing Larsa's meagre support and alleged attacks on his territory, and annexed the kingdom in 1763 BCE, gaining the whole lower Mesopotamian plain. A victory over Eshnunna, Shubartum and Gutium is commemorated in the name of his 32nd year. He then made war on Zimri-Lim: Mari was captured and destroyed between 1761 and 1759 BCE, and Malgium suffered a similar fate. Later year names record the defeat of a northern coalition and deportations from the conquered lands; in the process he established his rule over Assur. His titles grew from “king of Babylon” to “king of the four regions” of the world.

The king dug canals, among them one completed in his 33rd year and named “Hammurabi (brings) abundance to the people”, rebuilt the walls of Sippar and restored sanctuaries. Just over 200 of his letters survive, more than for any other Mesopotamian king; about a hundred are addressed to Sin-iddinam, governor of Larsa, on irrigation, troops, taxes, corvée labour and legal cases, and they show the king involving himself directly in provincial affairs and answering petitions from his subjects.

The Code of Hammurabi, written towards the end of the reign and known mainly from a large stele, has a prologue, an epilogue and what modern historians divide into 282 provisions on judicial practice, property, agriculture, finance, family law, assault, the professions and slaves. It is not the oldest Mesopotamian collection of laws, but it is the longest known.

By Hammurabi's death Babylon was the dominant power in Mesopotamia, but the unification was brief. Samsu-iluna lost the former territories of Larsa to revolts and gained nothing lasting in the north, and the dynasty, pressed by the First Sealand dynasty and by Kassite dynasties, was ended by a Hittite attack in 1595 BCE. Hammurabi can nevertheless be considered to have created the basis of a unified Lower Mesopotamia, reducing the old royal capitals to provincial towns.

He was declared a god in his own lifetime, and the personal name Hammurabi-ili, “Hammurabi is my god”, became common. Writings from shortly after his death commemorate him for victory, peace and justice; later the lawgiver came to overshadow the conqueror. Scribes went on copying his laws for centuries as writing exercises, the kings of Suhum claimed him as an ancestor more than a thousand years later, and a Neo-Babylonian inscription presents its king as a second Hammurabi.

His name re-emerged in the mid-19th century with the excavation of Mesopotamian sites. Joachim Menant published the first collection of his texts in 1863, and in 1901–1902 a French team unearthed the stele of the Code at Susa, its inscription being translated and published at once by Jean-Vincent Scheil. An early twentieth-century identification with Amraphel of Genesis 14:1 is now largely rejected. He is one of the 23 lawgivers shown in the chamber of the U.S. House of Representatives, and Saddam Hussein placed a bronze statue of him, over 4 metres high, at the entrance to the Iraqi Parliament.

Suleiman was born at Trabzon, on the southern coast of the Black Sea, probably on 6 November 1494, although the date is not known with certainty. His father was Şehzade Selim, the later Sultan Selim I; his mother, Hafsa Sultan, was a concubine and convert to Islam of unknown origins, who died in 1534. At the age of seven he began to study science, history, literature, theology and military tactics in the schools of the Topkapı Palace in Constantinople.

At seventeen he was appointed governor, first of Kaffa (Theodosia) and then of Manisa, with a brief tenure at Edirne. At Manisa the concubine Mahidevran entered his harem, and his first sons were born there, among them Mustafa in about 1516 or 1517. As a young man he befriended Ibrahim, originally a Christian from Parga in Epirus, who had been captured in a raid during the Ottoman–Venetian War of 1499–1503 and was given to Suleiman as a slave, most likely in 1514. Ibrahim converted to Islam, and Suleiman made him royal falconer and then first officer of the Royal Bedchamber.

The empire he was to inherit had been built by nine sultans before him. His great-grandfather Mehmed II had failed to take Belgrade because of John Hunyadi's defence, and after the defeats of the Albanians, Bosniaks, Bulgarians, Byzantines and Serbs, the Hungarians and Croats remained the only strong force that could block further Ottoman gains in Europe. His father, Selim I, who reigned from 1512 to 1520 and wrote poetry in Persian, had made war with the Shia Safavids of Persia a high priority.

Haile Selassie was born Tafari Makonnen on 23 July 1892 in the village of Ejersa Goro, in the Hararghe province of Ethiopia. As a child he was known as Lij Tafari Makonnen; the name Haile Selassie, "Power of the Trinity" in Ge'ez, was given to him at his infant baptism. His father, Ras Makonnen Wolde Mikael, was a grandson of King Sahle Selassie of Shewa and a general of the First Italo–Ethiopian War who had a large part in the Battle of Adwa. His mother, Woizero Yeshimebet Ali Abba Jifar, was the daughter of a ruling chief from Were Ilu in Wollo province. Through his paternal grandmother, an aunt of Emperor Menelik II, he belonged to the Solomonic dynasty, whose tradition traces every monarch to Menelik I, described in the Kebra Nagast as the son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba.

Ras Makonnen arranged for Tafari and his first cousin Imru Haile Selassie to be taught in Harar by Abba Samuel Wolde Kahin, an Ethiopian Capuchin friar, and by Dr. Vitalien, a surgeon from Guadeloupe. On 1 November 1905, at the age of 13, Tafari was named Dejazmach, a title roughly equivalent to count. His father died at Kulibi in 1906. Tafari assumed the titular governorship of Selale in 1906, was appointed governor over part of Sidamo in 1907, and was made governor of Harar in 1910 or 1911. It is alleged that in his late teens he was married to Woizero Altayech and that his daughter Princess Romanework was born of this union. On 3 August 1911 he married Menen Asfaw of Ambassel, niece of the heir to the throne, Lij Iyasu; the marriage lasted 50 years.

Haile Selassie is widely considered a defining figure in modern Ethiopian history, and his legacy remains a topic of debate. He helped to found Addis Ababa University and the Organisation of African Unity, the precursor of the African Union. His 1936 speech made him an icon for anti-fascists around the world, and he is remembered as a prominent anti-colonial leader. In the 1950s he was widely regarded as a modernising and capable ruler; in the 1970s famine and economic turmoil damaged that reputation. The Derg accused him of hoarding millions in Swiss banks, and Ethiopian media in 1974 claimed a fortune of 11 billion dollars, though records put his net worth at £22,000 as late as 1959. In recent years there has been a resurgence of nostalgia for his reign and of support for constitutional monarchy.

In Rastafari, a religion that emerged in Jamaica in the 1930s after news of his coronation arrived there, he is accorded divine importance; among adherents he is called the returned Jesus and the messiah who will lead the peoples of Africa and its diaspora to freedom. He was himself an adherent of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. When he visited Jamaica on 21 April 1966, approximately one hundred thousand Rastafari met him at the airport, a day commemorated as Grounation Day. In a 1967 interview he denied his alleged divinity, though many Rastafari do not read it as a denial. Most Rastafari rejected the funeral of 2000 and did not accept that the bones were his.

Washington is commonly known as the Father of His Country. Henry Lee III eulogised him as "first in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen", and polls have consistently placed him among the highest-ranked presidents. The precedents he set endured: republicanism, a peaceful transfer of power, the title "Mr. President", the cabinet and the two-term tradition. His resignation of his command in 1783 was, in the words of the historian Edward J. Larson, "extolled by later historians as a signal event that set the country's political course". As leader of the first successful revolution against a colonial empire he became an international symbol of liberation and nationalism.

He has been extensively memorialised. The national capital was named for him in 1791, as were a state, the 555-foot Washington Monument dedicated in 1885, and many schools and universities; he appears on Mount Rushmore, on the one-dollar bill and on the quarter. Congress made his birthday a federal holiday in 1879, and in 1976 he was posthumously appointed General of the Armies of the United States. The biography that Mason Locke Weems wrote in 1809 spread what Chernow calls "enduring myths", such as the story of the cherry tree. In the 21st century his reputation has been critically scrutinised. The historian David Hackett Fischer defined his character as "integrity, self-discipline, courage, absolute honesty, resolve, and decision"; others stress his slaveholding and, in Calloway's account, the dispossession of Indian peoples that the nation's growth demanded.

Liliʻuokalani began her reign by requiring the resignation of her brother's cabinet, a step the Supreme Court upheld with one dissent. On 9 March 1891 she named her niece Kaʻiulani as successor, and from April to July she toured the main islands. Her husband, made Prince Consort and restored as Governor of Oʻahu, died on 27 August 1891. From May 1892 to January 1893 the legislature sat for a record 171 days, divided among four parties; under the constitution of 1887 it could dismiss her ministers, and it voted out four of her cabinets.

From early in her reign she received petitions to rewrite the Bayonet Constitution, a demand supported by two-thirds of the registered voters. With the legislators Joseph Nāwahī and William Pūnohu White she drafted a constitution that would have restored power to the monarchy and voting rights to economically disenfranchised Native Hawaiians and Asians. On 13 January 1893 she appointed a cabinet chosen to support its promulgation, but her ministers withheld their backing, and on 16 January she and her supporters abandoned the attempt to proclaim it unilaterally. She was deposed the next day. She yielded her authority temporarily to the United States, not to the provisional government, in the hope that Washington would restore Hawaiian sovereignty. She was also an author and songwriter: she wrote "Aloha ʻOe", translated the creation chant Kumulipo, published in 1897, and set out her view of her country's history in Hawaiʻi's Story by Hawaiʻi's Queen (1898).
Legendary mother city of the Latins in the Alban Hills, remembered by the Romans as the home of Romulus and Remus and the seat of the Latin festival.

They lived in large fortified towns with grid-like streets, governed by councils and elected war leaders. [[e:numantia|Numantia's]] pottery shows painted horses and warriors. Herding, cereal growing and iron working sustained them, and Roman sources credit their warriors with courage and skill with the sword.
A Malwa dynasty of Dashapura whose king Yashodharman claimed victory over the Huns and rule from the Himalaya to the ocean.
The city-state of Attica that created democracy, led the Delian League and produced the drama, philosophy and architecture central to Classical Greek culture.

The coup of 1964 against [[e:joao-goulart|João Goulart]] ended the [[s:fourth-brazilian-republic|Fourth Brazilian Republic]]. Marshal [[e:humberto-castelo-branco|Humberto Castelo Branco]] became the first of five generals who ruled as president. [[e:institutional-acts|Institutional Acts]] gave the regime extraordinary powers, abolished the old parties and created two official ones, ARENA and the [[e:brazilian-democratic-movement|MDB]].

Their land was rich in iron ore, and the Bituriges were known as smiths and metalworkers. [[e:avaricum|Avaricum]], defended by a massive [[e:timber|timber]]-laced murus gallicus rampart, was one of the largest and wealthiest oppida in [[e:gaul|Gaul]].

The [[e:adil-shah|Adil Shahs]] alternated between Shia and [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] allegiance and employed Persian, African and [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] officers; [[e:shahaji-bhonsle|Shahaji Bhonsle]], father of [[e:shivaji|Shivaji]], served them. [[e:ibrahim-adil-shah-ii|Ibrahim Adil Shah II]] was a musician and patron of the arts, author of the [[e:kitab-i-nauras|Kitab-i-Nauras]]. [[e:bijapur|Bijapur's]] [[e:ibrahim-rauza|Ibrahim Rauza]] and the [[e:gol-gumbaz|Gol Gumbaz]], tomb of [[e:muhammad-adil-shah|Muhammad Adil Shah]], stand out in its architecture.
A Kurdish emirate that founded the city of Sulaymaniyah and became an early centre of Sorani Kurdish literature between the Ottoman and Persian empires.
The Alpine county that controlled the Mont Cenis and Great St Bernard passes, the origin of the house of Savoy and of later Italian kings.

The counts ruled a loosely held territory of powerful [[e:vassal|vassals]] and self-governing towns, where [[e:toulouse|Toulouse]] was run by elected consuls. Count [[e:raymond-iv-of-toulouse|Raymond IV]] led a great army on the [[e:first-crusade|First Crusade]] and founded the [[s:county-of-tripoli|County of Tripoli]]. The court encouraged troubadour poetry, and the [[e:catharism|Cathar]] heresy spread widely in its lands.

Croton produced more Olympic victors than any other city in some periods, above all the wrestler [[e:milo-of-croton|Milo]]. It was known for medicine, with [[e:democedes|Democedes]] and [[e:alcmaeon-of-croton|Alcmaeon]]. Around 530 BCE [[e:pythagoras|Pythagoras]] settled there, and his followers dominated politics for a time before being violently overthrown. The sanctuary of [[e:temple-of-hera-lacinia|Hera Lacinia]] at [[e:capo-colonna|Capo Colonna]] was a religious centre for the Italiote [[e:greeks|Greeks]]. After defeat by [[s:locri-epizephyrii|Locri]] at the [[e:battle-of-the-sagra|Sagras]] river, Croton crushed [[s:sybaris|Sybaris]] in 510 BCE.
The western successor of the Koch kingdom of northern Bengal, a princely state known for its cultured Maharajas until it joined India in 1949.
A Maya province of eastern Yucatán centred on Tihosuco, conquered in 1544, in whose region the Caste War later began.

Its paramount [[e:cacique|cacique]] [[e:caonabo|Caonabo]], said by some sources to have come from the Lucayan islands, was known as a war leader. His wife [[e:anacaona|Anacaona]] was the sister of [[e:bohechio|Bohechío]] of [[s:cacicazgo-of-jaragua|Jaragua]], linking the two [[e:chiefdom|chiefdoms]]. Its people farmed [[e:cassava|cassava]], held ballgames in plazas and worshipped zemís.

Pavia had been the capital of the [[s:kingdom-of-the-lombards|Kingdom of the Lombards]] and the coronation city of the [[s:kingdom-of-italy-medieval|Kingdom of Italy (medieval)]]. Around 1100 its citizens organised a commune under consuls, inheriting the city's royal palace traditions and a well-known school of law.
The rival government that Sun Yat-sen set up in Guangzhou to defend the constitution against Beijing's warlords, where the Nationalist revolution began.

The government depended on [[e:guangxi|Guangxi]] and [[e:yunnan|Yunnan]] generals, who forced Sun out in 1918 and ruled through a directorate under [[e:cen-chunxuan|Cen Chunxuan]]. [[e:chen-jiongming|Chen Jiongming]] brought Sun back in 1920, and in 1921 he became extraordinary president, but Chen turned against him in 1922. Returning in 1923, Sun accepted Soviet aid, admitted Communists to his party and founded the [[e:whampoa-military-academy|Whampoa Military Academy]] under [[e:chiang-kai-shek|Chiang Kai-shek]] in 1924.
Guild-ruled city-republic on Lake Zürich that joined the Swiss Confederacy in 1351 and in which Zwingli's Reformation.
